<explanation>

1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - ReqLLM is an Elixir library (not a standalone front-end/back-end app) that provides a unified, plugin-based interface for interacting with large language model (LLM) providers via HTTP.  
   - It builds on the Req HTTP client, adds typed data structures, streaming support, and a provider plugin architecture to simplify calls to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, xAI, OpenRouter, and more.

2. High-Level Architectural Overview  
   - Core Library Modules (in `lib/req_llm/`)  
     • Context & Message builders (compose system/user prompts)  
     • Model metadata & schema definitions  
     • Provider plugin framework (registry, DSL, option translators)  
     • Capability modules (generation, embeddings, streaming, tool-calling)  
     • Response processing & usage extraction  
     • Utility modules (key management, codecs, JSON encoders)  
   - Mix Tasks (in `lib/mix/tasks/`):  
     • `model_sync`: auto-sync metadata from models.dev into JSON files under `priv/models_dev/`  
     • `stream_text`: a CLI helper for streaming text from the command line  
   - External Services:  
     • LLM Providers (via HTTP REST endpoints)  
     • models.dev API (for model metadata sync)  

3. Main Components and Their Relationships  
   - Client API Layer (public functions like `generate_text/3`, `stream_text/3`, `embed_many/2`)  
     → Builds a `ReqLLM.Context` struct and selects a `ReqLLM.Model`.  
   - Provider Plugin Layer  
     → `ReqLLM.Provider.Registry` resolves the correct provider module (e.g., `ReqLLM.Providers.OpenAI`).  
     → Uses a Provider DSL and `ContextCodec` to translate internal structs into provider-specific HTTP payloads.  
   - Req HTTP Pipeline  
     → The provider module attaches middleware and executes `Req.request/1`.  
     → Streaming calls produce a `Stream` of `ReqLLM.StreamChunk` entries.  
   - Response Handling  
     → Raw JSON from HTTP response is decoded into Elixir structs (`Response`, `Usage`, content parts, etc.).  
     → Cost and token usage are extracted into a `ReqLLM.Usage` struct.  
     → Result is returned to the caller (either `{:ok, struct}` or raised on `!` variants).  
   - Model Metadata Management  
     → `mix req_llm.models.sync` fetches metadata from models.dev, writes to `priv/models_dev/*.json`.  
     → On startup (`ReqLLM.Application`), metadata JSON is loaded into memory for auto-sync and option validation.  

4. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles  
   - Plugin Architecture: providers implement a common behavior (`ReqLLM.Plugin`) and register themselves, enabling easy extension.  
   - Composability: builds on Req’s middleware pipeline for tracing, instrumentation, and custom middleware injection.  
   - Typed Data Structures: every call, response, and intermediate piece is a well-defined struct that can be serialized.  
   - Separation of Concerns: split into context construction, provider translation, HTTP transport, and response decoding.  
   - Mix Tasks for operational concerns (metadata sync, CLI tooling).  

5. Tailoring the Diagram to ReqLLM  
   - Emphasize the core library vs. the external HTTP world.  
   - Show the plugin registry as a central hub linking model calls to provider modules.  
   - Depict the flow from public API → context/model builder → provider codec → Req HTTP client → LLM REST API → back through codec → response structs → client.  
   - Highlight `priv/models_dev/` as a side datastore of model metadata, updated by a mix task.  

6. Diagramming Guidelines  
   - Components and Layers:  
     • Public API Layer  
     • Plugin Registry & DSL Layer  
     • HTTP Transport (Req Pipeline)  
     • External Services (LLM Providers, models.dev)  
     • Mix Tasks & Metadata Store  
   - Interactions:  
     • Use directional arrows to show request flow (API → context → provider → HTTP → LLM) and response flow back.  
     • Annotate streaming vs. non-streaming paths.  
   - Visual Distinctions:  
     • Color-code internal core modules (e.g., blue), provider plugins (green), external systems (orange), and mix tasks/metadata store (gray).  
     • Use different shapes: rectangles for modules, cylinders for data stores (`priv/models_dev`), clouds for external HTTP services.  
   - Labels:  
     • Clearly label each arrow with the operation (e.g., “attach middleware,” “serialize context,” “HTTP POST /chat”).  
     • Identify structs moving between layers (`Context`, `Model`, `Response`, `Usage`).  

7. Essential Diagram Elements Checklist  
   - Core library components split by folders (`Context`, `Provider`, `Response`, `Schema`, `Utils`).  
   - Plugin registry connecting to individual provider modules (OpenAI, Anthropic, ...).  
   - Req HTTP pipeline as the transport bus.  
   - External LLM APIs and models.dev API as separate, labeled clouds.  
   - Data store (`priv/models_dev/*.json`) showing the result of `mix req_llm.models.sync`.  
   - Mix tasks as operational tools outside the main request/response flow.  

By following these guidelines and tailoring your shapes, colors, labels, and arrows to the ReqLLM architecture, you will produce a clear, comprehensive system design diagram that captures both the high-level flow and the internal plugin-based structure of this Elixir library.  
</explanation>
